title: [READ VOL 9] Test 1 - Coins – the first form of money

parts.title: Coins – the first form of money
parts.passageHtml:
Coins – the first form of money

14 …………

Few people pay much attention to coins; we take them for granted. Since the advent of paper currency and the abandonment of a monetary system based on intrinsic of actual value, they have been demoted to the status of change: what is left when you have paid for something with 'paper' money. There is even a belief that they will one day be obsolete, as will paper or plastic notes, and money will at last have achieved the pure status of a mathematical formulation, a system of electronic credits and debits.

15 …………..

In the modern media environment, the sheer number of visual images is overwhelming, but it makes one stop to think that coins are among the most durable of our artefacts, and future archaeologists will scrutinise coins in order to learn about their distant ancestors. This is exactly the way ancient coins have informed us for over four millennia. There are thousands of different coins, each designed to carry meaning as well as value, tiny but rich sources of documentary evidence about events and cultural attitudes, frequently produced with exquisite craftsmanship.

16 ……………….

Coins in Europe date from 2,500 to 2,700 years ago, and seem to have originated in the ancient kingdom of Lydia, in what is now Turkey. Before coins, trade was based on barter: the direct trade of commodities. Barter required the physical presence of both commodities that were being traded. Metal coins were far more portable, and not subject to the same spoilage on long sea journeys as a commodity like grain might be if it became wet. However, they could also be accumulated, and these hoards could be stolen. Coins were therefore a temptation to criminals. The Greeks, however, were the first to realise the full potential of the new invention. They were a trading people of seafarers. Their civilisation, which was composed of dozens of city-states, was highly decentralised. Despite the potential for theft, the Greeks realised that they could benefit enormously from a system that used coins, because it meant that they no longer had to carry goods with them to barter.

17 …………….

The value of coins was generally based on the intrinsic value of the metal they were made of. At first this was mostly silver, and this meant that the discovery of silver mines on Greek territory actually increased the quantity of money they could produce. Had the Greek mining been on a larger scale, it could have caused problems similar to those faced by the Spanish centuries later, when so much gold from the New World was brought into their economy that it resulted in serious inflation. One advantage of intrinsic value was that coins could be weighed to determine the amount of metal they contained, so that the only thing an issuing state had to guarantee was the purity of the metal to prevent accusations of fraud and cheating, which could cause fighting and unrest. This was quite difficult to do, especially with coins made of gold, until Archimedes realised that different metals have different weight-volume ratios, and that by measuring the amount of displacement when coins were immersed in water, it was possible to establish whether gold was alloyed with silver.

18 ………………

All ancient coins were made by hand using engraved metal moulds. Many hundreds of coins were made, and as a result the moulds often cracked and new ones had to be engraved. This explains the endless variety encountered in coins with the same designs because the moulds had to be remade repeatedly, by many different artisans. One of the distinctive features of coins, in fact, is that they are the work of anonymous craftsmen, and yet each coin is an intimate reflection of the character of its city of origin. It was the Greeks who realised that coins could have a double function, as a unit of value and as a symbol of the identity of the city that issued them. The Greek view of life was deeply motivated by a spirit of competition, and coins, which circulated around the trading world, were a way of advertising the qualities of each particular city-state.

19 ……………………

Interestingly, Greek coins from the city of Athens, which was the home of the greatest sculptors of the classical period, seem to have been completely disconnected from the high sculptural tradition. The beautiful features of the city's patron, Athena (with her owl on the reverse of the coin), seem to have been repeated virtually unaltered for many years. Perhaps this was because the Athenian currency had grown increasingly to be the international standard and, like the US dollar today, a uniform design implied integrity.

20 ……………………

One side of a coin was always occupied by the head of a divinity, so it was a relatively small step, at around 323 BC, for Greek coins to replace that head with the portrait of the reigning monarch, a tradition that has continued in monarchies to the present day. Republics may have either symbolic heads – going back to the older tradition of divinities – or the features of a distinguished past head of state. The Romans adopted the Greek practice of coin design and as a result, the features of many great Romans have survived and are known to modern generations, despite the fact that the art of portrait painting was completely lost for more than a millennium following the fall of the Roman Empire.

questions.explanationHtml:
14. vii

Đoạn chứa đáp án:

There is even a belief that they will one day be obsolete, as will paper or plastic notes, and money will at last have achieved the pure status of a mathematical formulation, a system of electronic credits and debits.

Thậm chí còn có một niềm tin rằng một ngày nào đó chúng sẽ trở nên lỗi thời, giống như tiền giấy hay tiền nhựa, và tiền tệ cuối cùng sẽ đạt đến trạng thái thuần túy của một công thức toán học – một hệ thống các khoản ghi có và ghi nợ điện tử.

15. xi

Đoạn chứa đáp án:

This is exactly the way ancient coins have informed us for over four millennia. There are thousands of different coins, each designed to carry meaning as well as value, tiny but rich sources of documentary evidence about events and cultural attitudes, frequently produced with exquisite craftsmanship.

Đây chính xác là cách mà các đồng tiền cổ đã cung cấp thông tin cho chúng ta trong suốt hơn bốn thiên niên kỷ. Có hàng nghìn loại tiền xu khác nhau, mỗi loại đều được thiết kế không chỉ để mang giá trị mà còn truyền tải ý nghĩa, là những nguồn tư liệu nhỏ bé nhưng phong phú về các sự kiện và thái độ văn hóa, thường được chế tác với tay nghề tinh xảo.

16. v

Đoạn chứa đáp án:

Metal coins were far more portable, and not subject to the same spoilage on long sea journeys as a commodity like grain might be if it became wet.

Tiền kim loại dễ mang theo hơn nhiều và không bị hư hỏng trong những chuyến đi biển dài như các loại hàng hóa như ngũ cốc có thể bị nếu bị ẩm ướt.

17. iv

Đoạn chứa đáp án:

The value of coins was generally based on the intrinsic value of the metal they were made of.

Giá trị của tiền xu thường dựa trên giá trị nội tại của kim loại dùng để chế tạo ra chúng.

18. ii

Đoạn chứa đáp án:

The Greek view of life was deeply motivated by a spirit of competition, and coins, which circulated around the trading world, were a way of advertising the qualities of each particular city-state.

Quan niệm sống của người Hy Lạp chịu ảnh hưởng sâu sắc bởi tinh thần cạnh tranh, và tiền xu – lưu hành khắp thế giới buôn bán – là một cách để quảng bá những đặc điểm, thế mạnh riêng của từng thành bang.

19. ix

Đoạn chứa đáp án:

The beautiful features of the city's patron, Athena (with her owl on the reverse of the coin), seem to have been repeated virtually unaltered for many years. Perhaps this was because the Athenian currency had grown increasingly to be the international standard and, like the US dollar today, a uniform design implied integrity.

Những đường nét tuyệt đẹp của nữ thần bảo hộ thành phố, Athena (với hình con cú ở mặt sau đồng xu), dường như đã được lặp lại gần như không thay đổi trong nhiều năm. Có lẽ điều này là do tiền tệ của Athens ngày càng trở thành tiêu chuẩn quốc tế và, giống như đồng đô la Mỹ ngày nay, một thiết kế thống nhất thể hiện tính toàn vẹn.

20. vi

Đoạn chứa đáp án:

One side of a coin was always occupied by the head of a divinity, so it was a relatively small step, at around 323 BC, for Greek coins to replace that head with the portrait of the reigning monarch, a tradition that has continued in monarchies to the present day. Republics may have either symbolic heads – going back to the older tradition of divinities – or the features of a distinguished past head of state. The Romans adopted the Greek practice of coin design and as a result, the features of many great Romans have survived and are known to modern generations, despite the fact that the art of portrait painting was completely lost for more than a millennium following the fall of the Roman Empire.

Một mặt của đồng xu luôn được khắc hình đầu của một vị thần, vì vậy, vào khoảng năm 323 trước Công nguyên, việc Hy Lạp thay thế hình đầu đó bằng chân dung của vị vua trị vì trên đồng xu là một bước tiến tương đối nhỏ, một truyền thống đã được các chế độ quân chủ tiếp tục cho đến ngày nay. Các nước cộng hòa có thể sử dụng hình ảnh tượng trưng – quay trở lại truyền thống cổ xưa về các vị thần – hoặc hình ảnh của một nguyên thủ quốc gia lỗi lạc trong quá khứ. Người La Mã đã tiếp thu cách thiết kế tiền xu của người Hy Lạp và kết quả là, chân dung của nhiều người La Mã vĩ đại đã được lưu giữ và biết đến bởi các thế hệ hiện đại, mặc dù nghệ thuật vẽ chân dung đã hoàn toàn bị thất truyền trong hơn một thiên niên kỷ sau sự sụp đổ của Đế chế La Mã.

questions.text: 21-22 Which TWO of these comments about ancient coins are made by the writer of the text?
questions.explanationHtml:
21-22. C, A

Câu hỏi: Which TWO of these comments about ancient coins are made by the writer of the text?

A. There is no record of the names of the coin makers. B. Coins were not popular as payment for traded objects. C. Coins with the same design often looked quite different. D. Greek coins were more beautiful in design than Roman coins. E. At times, too many coins were produced in Greece.

(Hai trong số những nhận xét sau đây về tiền xu cổ được tác giả của văn bản đưa ra? A. Không có ghi chép nào về tên của những người đúc tiền. B. Tiền xu không phổ biến như một phương tiện thanh toán cho các vật phẩm được giao dịch. C. Những đồng tiền có cùng thiết kế thường trông khá khác nhau. D. Tiền xu Hy Lạp có thiết kế đẹp hơn tiền xu La Mã. E. Đôi khi, Hy Lạp sản xuất quá nhiều tiền xu.)

Đoạn chứa đáp án:

This explains the endless variety encountered in coins with the same designs because the moulds had to be remade repeatedly, by many different artisans. One of the distinctive features of coins, in fact, is that they are the work of anonymous craftsmen, and yet each coin is an intimate reflection of the character of its city of origin.

Điều này giải thích sự đa dạng gần như vô tận của các đồng tiền có cùng thiết kế, bởi vì các khuôn đúc phải được làm lại nhiều lần bởi nhiều nghệ nhân khác nhau. Thực tế, một trong những đặc điểm nổi bật của tiền xu là chúng là sản phẩm của những người thợ vô danh, nhưng mỗi đồng tiền lại phản ánh một cách gần gũi bản sắc của thành phố nơi nó được tạo ra.

Đoạn chứa đáp án:

The value of coins was generally based on the intrinsic value of the metal they were made of. At first this was mostly silver, and this meant that the discovery of silver mines on Greek territory actually increased the quantity of money they could produce.
